common_name: Little Quick Fire Hydrangea (Compact Early-Blooming Panicle Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Little Quick Fire is roughly two-thirds the size of the original Quick Fire, fitting foundation plantings and smaller borders where the full-size selection would quickly outgrow the space.

directions: Little Quick Fire is a compact sport of Quick Fire hydrangea, keeping the same early bloom timing and unusually fast color change but on a dense, rounded shrub well under half the mature size of most panicle hydrangeas. White flower panicles open several weeks ahead of standard panicle hydrangeas in early summer, then shift to pink and finally deep wine-red within weeks, giving a long season of color change on sturdy stems that hold the flower heads upright without staking. Like other panicle hydrangeas it blooms on new wood, so it tolerates a hard late-winter pruning to control size or renew an aging plant without sacrificing the coming season's bloom, and it takes more sun than mophead hydrangeas without wilting.

common_name: Lemon Lime Nandina (Bright Chartreuse Compact Heavenly Bamboo)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; foliage color is brightest with several hours of direct sun, while some afternoon shade helps prevent scorch in peak Gulf South summer heat.

directions: Lemon Lime is a dwarf, mounding nandina selected for foliage that emerges bright chartreuse-lime rather than the red tones typical of most nandina cultivars, holding that fresh lime-green color through summer without the burgundy winter shift seen in other dwarf types. Its compact, dense habit and unusual color make it a useful accent for brightening a shaded bed or breaking up the heavier greens and burgundies of a typical foundation planting. Like other modern dwarf nandina selections it is sterile and produces no berries, avoiding the self-seeding that has made standard nandina invasive in parts of the Southeast, and it needs little pruning beyond removing occasional damaged canes.

common_name: Harbor Dwarf Nandina (Classic Spreading Groundcover Heavenly Bamboo)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to full shade; Harbor Dwarf is one of the most shade-tolerant nandina selections and spreads gradually by underground rhizomes to form a dense, low groundcover.

directions: Harbor Dwarf is one of the longest-established and most reliable dwarf nandina cultivars, a low, spreading selection grown as a mass groundcover under trees, along foundations, and on slopes where its rhizomatous spread gradually knits together into a dense, weed-suppressing mat. New foliage emerges bronze-red and matures to blue-green through the growing season before turning red-orange in winter cold, giving reliable color change with almost no maintenance beyond an occasional cutting back of old canes. It tolerates deep shade better than most nandina selections, making it a dependable evergreen filler for difficult dry shade under mature trees, and unlike straight-species nandina it fruits only sparsely, reducing (though not eliminating) self-seeding.

common_name: Double Play Gold Spirea (Reblooming Gold-Foliage Compact Spirea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; best foliage color develops in full sun, and deadheading the first flush of flowers encourages the summer rebloom that gives this series its name.

directions: Double Play Gold is a compact, part of Proven Winners' reblooming Double Play spirea series, valued for bright gold foliage that emerges with orange-red tints in spring and holds its color through summer, topped by rounded clusters of pink flowers. Unlike older spirea cultivars that bloom in one spring flush, Double Play selections rebloom through summer, especially if the spent flower clusters are sheared off after the first round fades, giving a longer season of both foliage and flower interest from a low, tidy mound. It is extremely tough and low-maintenance, tolerating drought, heat, and poor soil once established, and a single light shearing after the first bloom flush is usually all the pruning it needs.

common_name: Blush Pink Nandina (Soft Pink New-Growth Compact Heavenly Bamboo)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; new-growth color is most vivid with several hours of direct sun, while afternoon shade helps prevent leaf scorch in the hottest part of the Gulf South summer.

directions: Blush Pink is a dwarf, mounding nandina selected for new foliage that emerges soft candy-pink before maturing to green, giving a softer, pastel-toned flush of color than the red new growth typical of most dwarf nandina cultivars. Its compact, dense habit fits foundation plantings and mixed containers, and the plant is sterile, producing no berries and avoiding the self-seeding that has made standard nandina an invasive problem in parts of the Southeast. Little pruning beyond removing occasional damaged canes is needed to keep its naturally tidy shape.
